props.title: Infinity

sections.content: **Infinity** (1996) stands as Matthew Broderick's directorial debut, tackling the early life of theoretical physicist Richard Feynman with surprising intimacy. Unlike traditional science biopics like **A Beautiful Mind** (2001) or **The Theory of Everything** (2014), Broderick focuses tightly on Feynman's romance with his first wife Arline Greenbaum and their heart-wrenching journey through her tuberculosis diagnosis, set against the backdrop of the Manhattan Project. The film captures Feynman's unique approach to both science and life, showcasing his playful curiosity alongside deep emotional complexity.

sections.content: The 1990s saw a surge of science-focused biographical films that attempted to humanize great minds. **October Sky** (1999) examined the inspiring story of NASA engineer Homer Hickam, while **IQ** (1994) took a more romantic comedy approach to Einstein's later years. **Infinity** distinguishes itself by avoiding the typical "genius at work" tropes, instead examining how love and scientific pursuit can coexist in times of extreme pressure and personal crisis. SUBHEAD: The Human Side of Scientific Achievement

What makes **Infinity** particularly noteworthy is its handling of the Manhattan Project's moral weight. Unlike **Fat Man and Little Boy** (1989) or **Day One** (1989), which focus on the project's broader ethical implications, Broderick's film uses this momentous scientific endeavor as a backdrop for a deeply personal story. The approach mirrors later films like **The Imitation Game** (2014), which balanced Alan Turing's technical achievements with his personal struggles, though **Infinity** maintains an even more intimate focus.
